metadata.file_name: Achieving the same educational opportunities for all  overcoming hoax interpretations of the PISA results.pdf
metadata.title: Achieving the same educational opportunities for all: overcoming hoax interpretations of the PISA results
metadata.venue: International Journal of Adolescence and Youth

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study is a single-school case study in Spain using school-level documentary data (absenteeism reports and Basic Competences test results in 6th grade primary). Although the paper references PISA 2023 as a contextual benchmark for interpreting hoax-like claims, the empirical analyses reported are not conducted on the OECD/PISA microdata and do not describe the use of PISA sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures. The paper does not report any survey-weight variable names (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or any complex-survey variance estimation approach; therefore, no ILSA-style weighted estimation can be confirmed from the methods section. The reported comparisons are across school years (2013–2014, 2020–2021, 2022–2023) and across Basic Competences domains, with no stated PV-based scaling or IRT/PV estimation workflow.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study does not model cognitive achievement using PISA-style Plausible Values (PV) or report an ILSA PV-based scoring/estimation pipeline; instead, it reports school Basic Competences pass rates and absenteeism percentages over time. Because the dependent outcomes are not PV-based achievement scores, PV handling is not applicable. The paper also does not describe any missing-data procedure for the documentary school records (e.g., how missing absenteeism entries or test-result gaps were treated), so missing-data handling is not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The empirical dataset is a single school in a vulnerable area of Spain (Catalonia) with Basic Competences results in 6th grade primary and school absenteeism records. The paper does not report an analytic sample size or a student-level inclusion/exclusion rule (e.g., number of students tested, missing test forms, or exclusions). The only explicit temporal selection is the use of three school years (2013–2014, 2020–2021, 2022–2023) and the focus on 6th grade primary for academic results; absenteeism is reported for educational cycles (ECEC, primary, secondary) with detailed grade breakdown only for 2021–2022 and 2022–2023.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2023 as a contextual benchmark for interpretin the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This article is a qualitative-quantitative case study rather than an empirical machine-learning prediction paper. It uses school documentary data from a marginalized neighbourhood in Catalonia, Spain, focusing on absenteeism and Basic Competences outcomes in 6th grade primary across three school years (2013–2014, 2020–2021, 2022–2023). The paper reports improvements in pass rates in language (Catalan, Spanish, English) and in mathematics and natural sciences, alongside a reduction in absenteeism from 50% (2009–2010) to 16% (2022–2023), and it links these changes to the implementation of Successful Educational Actions (SEA) and dialogic learning principles. No ML model training, PV-based achievement modeling, or survey-weighted estimation is described; therefore, no predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE/AUC) are available. The main limitation is that the evidence is not based on a controlled design and does not provide student-level sample sizes or missing-data handling procedures. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse for ML-specific fields because the manuscript does not present a machine-learning modeling pipeline (no algorithms, no target-variable prediction/classification, and no reported predictive metrics). It also does not provide student-level sample sizes or per-country counts, because the empirical evidence is drawn from a single school’s internal records rather than from an international ILSA microdata extract. As a result, PV handling, missing-data handling, and weighting are not operationalized in the way they would be for an ILSA-based empirical ML study.
